newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Political, financial woes slam S.Korean businesses.
newsitem.headline: Political, financial woes slam S.Korean businesses.

text.p: A corporate sleaze scandal dragged in another South Korean conglomerate on Wednesday, and a chain of bankruptcies claimed a new victim, driving the stock market down.
The Chosun Ilbo newspaper said prosecutors were probing the 16th ranked Hansol Group, widening a political corruption scandal involving President Kim Young-sam's son.
That news combined with the failure of a leading woollen textile maker, Yu Sung Co Ltd, spooked investors and touched off selling among a slew of beleaguered companies.
At the close of trading, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index had dropped 1.78 percent or 12.47 points to 689.10.
Investors dumped shares of Hansol's seven listed companies. All fell sharply.
Hansol Paper, group flagship and the country's largest paper maker, tumbled 1,700 won ($1.9) to its limit low of 19,600. Hansol Electron also went limit-down, falling 1,900 won to 22,400.
The Chosun Ilbo said state prosecutors had evidence that the group managed a seven billion won fund for presidential son Kim Hyun-chul.
Later, the main opposition National Congress for New Politics alleged the money was part of a 20 billion won fund left over from President Kim Young-sam's 1992 election.
The Hansol Group issued a vaguely-worded statement apparently in response to the Chosun Ilbo report.

"Talk about an influx of funds into the Hansol Group is not true," the statement quoted group information director Kim Jung-bo as saying. "There seems to be a big misunderstanding. I hope the prosecution will uncover the truth."
Kim Hyun-chul is being investigated by prosecutors for his role in a loans-for-kickback scandal involving a failed steelmaker, Hanbo Steel Co.
Domestic newspapers have quoted prosecutors as saying Kim, the president's second son, will be arrested soon.

Speeding the market's fall was an announcement by Yu Sung that it had filed for court protection late on Tuesday. The company said it had defaulted on payments of 337 million won in promissory notes, and banks had frozen its checking accounts.
Yu Sung's finance manager said his company was hit by Korea's overall economic slowdown.
"We have temporary cash-flow problems," he said. "But we are sure we can survive under court receivership."

Yu Sung did not qualify for aid from a bank committee set up last month to keep troubled corporates afloat. That committee intervened to save the Jinro Group, but will only step in if a company's debt exceeds 250 billion won.
The collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January, followed by Sammi Steel Co in March and the near collapse of Jinro set off alarm bells in corporate Korea.
The Ssangyong and Doosan business groups recently announced plans to sell off real estate and merge or sell affiliates in an effort to pare costs by focusing on core businesses.
Korea First Bank, which is owed more than 1.2 trillion won by Hanbo Steel and Sammi Steel, this week said it would try to rescue itself by shedding subsidiaries and cutting salaries.
Doosan and Jinro shares took a pounding on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, the Finance and Economy Ministry said on Wednesday it had drafted legislation to establish a 1.5 trillion won fund to deal with corporate bankruptcies. The legislation would be submitted to parliament in June, it said.

The fund, to be operated by the state-run Korea Asset Management Corp, would be financed with bank contributions, bond issues and borrowings. The ministry estimated bad debts held by the nation's banks at 2.4 trillion won.
